chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Al-Husayn ibn Nueym, from Abu Al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who designated a house as a residence for a man during his lifetime, or designated it for him and his offspring after him. He said: 'It is for him and his offspring after him, as stipulated.' I said: 'So if he is in need, can he sell it?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'So does his sale revoke the residential house?' He said: 'The sale does not revoke the residence.' Thus, I heard my father (peace be upon him) saying. Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'The sale does not revoke the lease nor the residence, but it is sold on the condition that the one who buys it does not own what he bought until the residence is revoked, according to what was stipulated and the lease.' I said: 'So if he returns the money to the tenant, and all that was incumbent upon him regarding maintenance and construction for what he rented?' He said: 'With goodwill, and the tenant is pleased with that, there is no problem.'

key_terms.سُكْنَى: Residence / Habitation (a type of endowment or designation for living)

ai.seo_question: Can a house designated for lifelong residence be sold, and does the sale affect the tenant's rights?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the fiqh of 'Sukna' (lifetime habitation), establishing that while the property remains alienable, the right of residence is a binding encumbrance that survives the sale until its term expires. It highlights the Shia scholarly distinction between ownership and usufruct, noting that the new owner acquires the title subject to the existing tenancy unless the tenant voluntarily agrees to vacate with fair compensation.
